decks.title: Pythagoras Theorem — Part 1: The theorem and its area proof
goals: Name the hypotenuse and the legs of a right-angled triangle
State Pythagoras theorem and prove it by comparing areas
Find the hypotenuse or a leg of a right-angled triangle
Leave an answer as a square root or round it correctly

slides.heading: Pythagoras theorem, Part 1
slides.body_md: Draw a square on each side of a right-angled triangle. The two small squares together have **the same area as the big one**.

visual.alt: A right triangle with legs three and two units, with a square drawn outwards on each side. The squares on the legs have areas nine and four; the square on the longest side has area thirteen.
visual.caption: Areas of the three squares: 9 + 4 = 13.

slides.narration: Welcome. This chapter is about one of the most famous facts in geometry. Take a right angled triangle and draw a square on each of its three sides. The two smaller squares together have exactly the same area as the biggest square. In this first part we see why this is true, using areas only, and then use it to find missing sides.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: **Find** a missing side: a whole number, a decimal or a square root

visual.alt: Flow with four boxes: right-angled triangle, squares on the sides, areas add up, find a missing side. The arrows are labelled draw, prove and use.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four steps

slides.narration: By the end of this part you will name the sides of a right angled triangle, state Pythagoras theorem, and prove it by comparing areas. Then you will use it to find a missing side, as a whole number, a decimal or a square root. Part two turns the theorem around and uses it on ladders, diagonals and heights.

slides.heading: The sides of a right-angled triangle
slides.body_md: The side **opposite the right angle** is the **hypotenuse**. It is the **longest side**. The two sides that meet at the right angle are the **legs**.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle A B C with the right angle at B. The two sides that meet at the right angle are the legs, marked a and b. The side opposite the right angle, marked c, is the hypotenuse.
visual.caption: Legs a and b; hypotenuse c.

slides.narration: A right angled triangle has one angle of ninety degrees. The side opposite that angle is called the hypotenuse, and it is always the longest side. The other two sides, which meet at the right angle, are the legs. In the picture the legs are a and b, and the hypotenuse is c. Always find the right angle first, because it tells you which side is the hypotenuse.

slides.heading: Pythagoras theorem
slides.body_md:
**Theorem.** In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

$c^2 = a^2 + b^2$

visual.alt: A right triangle with legs three and two units, with a square drawn outwards on each side. The squares on the legs have areas nine and four; the square on the longest side has area thirteen.
visual.caption: Areas of the three squares: 9 + 4 = 13.

slides.narration: Here is the theorem. In a right angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. In the picture the legs are three and two units, so the squares on them have areas nine and four. The square on the hypotenuse has area thirteen, and nine plus four is thirteen. Remember, it is squares, not lengths, that add.

slides.heading: Reading the squares
slides.body_md: The **areas** add up, but the **lengths** do not: $3 + 2 = 5$, yet the hypotenuse is only about $3.6$.

headers: Area of the square on it

visual.alt: Table of the three squares on the sides of the triangle with legs three and two: the squares on the legs have areas nine and four and the square on the hypotenuse has area thirteen. The areas add up, but the lengths do not.

slides.narration: Let us read the picture as a table. The leg of length three has a square of area nine. The leg of length two has a square of area four. The hypotenuse has length square root of thirteen, which is about three point six, and its square has area thirteen. Nine plus four equals thirteen. The lengths do not add up, three plus two is five and not three point six, but the areas do.

slides.heading: Quick check: state the theorem
slides.body_md: Find the hypotenuse first, then pick the statement.
slides.narration: Triangle P Q R has its right angle at Q. Which statement is Pythagoras theorem for it? First find the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle. Then put its square on one side and the sum of the squares of the other two on the other side.

slides.heading: Plan of the proof
slides.body_md: We prove the theorem by counting one area in two ways.

nodes.label: Draw a square of side a + b
Place four right triangles in the corners
Show the middle shape is a square of side c
Count the big area in two ways
Simplify: a squared + b squared = c squared

visual.alt: Flow with five boxes: draw a square of side a plus b, place four right triangles in the corners, show the middle shape is a square of side c, count the big area in two ways, simplify to get a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
visual.caption: Plan of the area proof

slides.narration: Here is the plan of the proof. We draw a big square of side a plus b. We place four copies of the right triangle in its corners. We show that the shape left in the middle is a square whose side is the hypotenuse c. Then we count the area of the big square in two different ways. Setting the two counts equal, and simplifying, gives the theorem.

slides.heading: Proof, step 1: build the figure
slides.body_md: Take a right-angled triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$. Draw a square $ABCD$ of side $a + b$. On each side mark a point ($E$, $F$, $G$, $H$) so that the pieces are $a$ and $b$, going round in the same direction. Join the four points.

visual.alt: A big square A B C D with a point on each side: E on A B, F on B C, G on C D and H on D A. Joining E F G H cuts off four right triangles at the corners. Equal tick marks show the short sides are equal and the long sides are equal, and the four slanting sides E F, F G, G H, H E have three tick marks.
visual.caption: The big square has side a + b; the four triangles have legs a and b.

slides.narration: Take a right angled triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c. Draw a big square with side a plus b. On every side mark a point so that the two pieces are a and b, going round the square in the same direction. Join the four points. The tick marks show equal lengths. This cuts four corner triangles from the big square, and each one has legs a and b.

slides.heading: Proof, step 2: four congruent triangles
bullets: The four corner triangles each have legs $a$ and $b$ with a **right angle between them**
Hence the four slanting sides $EF$, $FG$, $GH$, $HE$ are **all equal**, each equal to the hypotenuse $c$

visual.alt: The same figure shaded: four right triangles in one shade and the tilted square E F G H in another.
visual.caption: Big square = four triangles + tilted square.

slides.narration: Look at the four corner triangles, shaded in the picture. Each has a right angle at a corner of the big square, with legs a and b on either side of it. So they are all congruent, by side, angle, side. It follows that the four slanting sides, E F, F G, G H and H E, are all equal. Each is the hypotenuse of a triangle with legs a and b, so each has length c.

slides.heading: Proof, step 3: the middle shape is a square
slides.body_md: In a corner triangle the acute angles are $x$ and $y$, and $x + y = 90^\circ$. At $E$ the angles $x$, $\angle HEF$ and $y$ lie on a straight line, so $\angle HEF = 180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$.

visual.alt: The same figure with the angle at E marked. The angle x of triangle A E H and the angle y of triangle B F E sit beside the angle H E F, and the angle H E F carries a right-angle mark.
visual.caption: The angles at E: x + y = 90, so the angle of the inner square is 90.

slides.narration: Now the angles. In a corner triangle the two acute angles, call them x and y, add up to ninety degrees, because the angles of a triangle add up to one hundred eighty and one of them is ninety. At the point E, the angle x, the angle of the middle shape, and the angle y lie along a straight line, so they add up to one hundred eighty. So the angle of the middle shape is one hundred eighty minus ninety, which is ninety degrees.

slides.heading: Proof, step 4: all the reasons
slides.body_md: The middle shape has **four equal sides** and **four right angles**, so it is a **square of side $c$**.

rows: two legs $a$ and $b$ with the right angle between them
angle sum of a corner triangle (one angle is $90^\circ$)
the angles $x$, $\angle HEF$ and $y$ lie on a straight line
four equal sides and four right angles

visual.alt: Table of five claims and reasons showing that the middle shape is a square of side c: congruent triangles, equal hypotenuses, x plus y is ninety degrees, the straight line gives ninety degrees, so it is a square.

slides.narration: Here are all the reasons together. The four corner triangles are congruent, so the four slanting sides are equal to c. The acute angles of a corner triangle add up to ninety degrees, so the straight line at each point leaves a right angle. Four equal sides and four right angles make a square. So the middle shape is a square of side c, and its area is c squared.

slides.heading: Proof, step 5: count the area twice
slides.body_md: Try it with $a = 3$ and $b = 5$.

visual.alt: Table counting the areas for legs three and five: the big square has area sixty four, the four triangles thirty, the middle square thirty four, and three squared plus five squared is also thirty four.

slides.narration: Let us count the area in two ways, using the legs three and five. The big square has side eight, so its area is sixty four. Each corner triangle has area seven and a half, so the four triangles have area thirty. The middle square is what is left, sixty four minus thirty, which is thirty four. And three squared plus five squared is nine plus twenty five, also thirty four. The rule works.

slides.heading: Proof, step 6: the algebra
slides.body_md: Now repeat the count with any legs $a$ and $b$.

rows: Four triangles and the middle square

visual.alt: Table of four algebra steps: the big square is a plus b all squared, the triangles and middle square give two a b plus c squared, equating and cancelling two a b gives a squared plus b squared equals c squared.

slides.narration: Now the algebra, with any legs a and b. The big square has area a plus b all squared, which expands to a squared plus two a b plus b squared. The four triangles have area two a b together, and the middle square has area c squared. Equating the two counts gives a squared plus two a b plus b squared equals two a b plus c squared. Cancel two a b from both sides, leaving a squared plus b squared equals c squared.

slides.heading: Quick check: the area equation
slides.body_md: Which equation counts the big square two ways?
slides.narration: Which equation comes from counting the big square area in two ways? Check that each term is an area, and that all four triangles are included.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the proof in numbers
slides.body_md: Legs $20$ and $21$: find the area of the big square, of the four triangles and of the middle square.

visual.alt: Table for legs twenty and twenty one: the big square has area one thousand six hundred eighty one, four triangles have area eight hundred forty, the middle square has area eight hundred forty one, which is twenty nine squared.

slides.narration: Test the proof with numbers. The legs are twenty and twenty one, so the big square has side forty one and area one thousand six hundred eighty one. Each triangle has area two hundred ten, so the four have area eight hundred forty. The middle square is one thousand six hundred eighty one minus eight hundred forty, which is eight hundred forty one. Also twenty squared plus twenty one squared is four hundred plus four hundred forty one, again eight hundred forty one, which is twenty nine squared.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tilted square
slides.body_md: Give an area, not a length.
slides.narration: Four triangles with legs twenty and twenty one sit inside a square of side forty one. What is the area of the tilted square? Count the area of the whole square, take away the four triangles, and take care to give an area, not a length.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: find the hypotenuse
slides.body_md: A right-angled triangle has legs $2.8$ cm and $4.5$ cm. Find the hypotenuse.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle with legs two point eight and four point five centimetres. The hypotenuse is to be found.
visual.caption: Legs 2.8 cm and 4.5 cm.

slides.narration: A right angled triangle has legs two point eight and four point five centimetres. Find the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse squared is two point eight squared plus four point five squared. That is seven point eight four plus twenty point two five, which is twenty eight point oh nine. The square root of twenty eight point oh nine is five point three, so the hypotenuse is five point three centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: find a leg
slides.body_md: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $8.5$ cm and one leg $3.6$ cm. Find the other leg.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle with hypotenuse eight point five centimetres and one leg three point six centimetres. The other leg is to be found.
visual.caption: Hypotenuse 8.5 cm, one leg 3.6 cm.

slides.narration: Now the hypotenuse is given. A right angled triangle has hypotenuse eight point five centimetres and one leg three point six centimetres. To find the other leg, subtract. The leg squared is eight point five squared minus three point six squared, which is seventy two point two five minus twelve point nine six, or fifty nine point two nine. So the leg is seven point seven centimetres. When the hypotenuse is known, we subtract.

slides.heading: Quick check: the middle shape
slides.body_md: Think about the sides and the angles we found.
slides.narration: True or false? The shape left in the middle of the big square is a square whose side is the hypotenuse. Think about the equal sides and the angles we found.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: not a perfect square
slides.body_md: A right-angled triangle has legs $7$ cm and $9$ cm. Find the hypotenuse.
bullets: **Step 2 —** $130$ lies between $11^2 = 121$ and $12^2 = 144$, so it is not a perfect square.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle with legs seven and nine centimetres. The hypotenuse is the square root of one hundred thirty.
visual.caption: The hypotenuse is not a whole number.

slides.narration: Sometimes the answer is not a whole number. A right angled triangle has legs seven and nine centimetres. The hypotenuse squared is forty nine plus eighty one, which is one hundred thirty. One hundred thirty is not a perfect square, because eleven squared is one hundred twenty one and twelve squared is one hundred forty four. So the hypotenuse is the square root of one hundred thirty centimetres, which is about eleven point four zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: only areas are given
slides.body_md: The squares on the hypotenuse and on one leg of a right-angled triangle have areas $289$ cm$^2$ and $225$ cm$^2$. Find the other leg.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Square on the other leg: $289 - 225 = 64$ cm$^2$.
**Answer —** The leg is $\sqrt{64} = 8$ cm; the sides are $8$, $15$, $17$.

visual.alt: Table with the squares on the sides of a right-angled triangle: hypotenuse area two hundred eighty nine with side seventeen, one leg area two hundred twenty five with side fifteen, and the other leg area sixty four with side eight.

slides.narration: In this example only areas are given. The square on the hypotenuse has area two hundred eighty nine square centimetres, and the square on one leg has area two hundred twenty five. The square on the other leg must make up the difference. Two hundred eighty nine minus two hundred twenty five is sixty four. So the other leg is the square root of sixty four, which is eight centimetres. The triangle has sides eight, fifteen and seventeen.

slides.heading: Summary of part 1
slides.body_md: Pythagoras theorem links the three sides of a right-angled triangle through **squares**.

rows: the side opposite the right angle; the longest side
big square of side $a + b$ = four triangles + a middle square of side $c$
leave a surd, or round at the end

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: the hypotenuse, Pythagoras theorem, the area proof, finding the hypotenuse by adding squares, finding a leg by subtracting squares, and what to do when the answer is not a perfect square.

slides.narration: Here is the summary of part one. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Pythagoras theorem says its square is the sum of the squares of the legs. We proved it by counting the area of a big square in two ways. To find the hypotenuse, add the squares. To find a leg, subtract. If the result is not a perfect square, leave a square root or round at the end. Part two reverses the theorem.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Proof (about 4 to 6 marks):** the figure with side $a + b$ 1, congruent triangles 1, middle shape is a square 1 or 2, the two area counts 1, the conclusion 1
**Finding a side (2 marks):** the equation 1 + the value with unit 1
**Always** say which side is the hypotenuse before you start
**Mistake:** adding when you should subtract, or the reverse

rows: subtracting when the hypotenuse is asked
add the squares for the hypotenuse; subtract for a leg
using a leg as the hypotenuse
the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle
take the square root at the end

visual.alt: Table of five common slips in part one and their corrections: adding lengths, subtracting when adding is needed, mixing up the hypotenuse, splitting a square root of a sum, and giving the square instead of the length.

slides.narration: Here is how marks are awarded. A proof is marked step by step: the figure with its sides, the congruent triangles, the reason the middle shape is a square, the two area counts, and the conclusion. For finding a side, one mark is for the equation and one for the value with its unit. Say which side is the hypotenuse before you start. The common slips are adding the lengths, and adding when you should subtract.

decks.title: Pythagoras Theorem — Part 2: The converse, triples and applications
goals: State the converse of Pythagoras theorem and use it to test for a right angle
Solve problems on ladders, diagonals and heights of triangles
Use the result for quadrilaterals with perpendicular diagonals

slides.heading: Pythagoras theorem, Part 2
slides.body_md: Now the other way round: if the **squares of the sides balance**, the triangle has a **right angle**.

visual.alt: A triangle A B C with A B twenty, B C twenty one and C A twenty nine centimetres. The angle at B is marked as a right angle.
visual.caption: Sides 20, 21, 29: a right angle at B.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. In part one we started with a right angle and found a relationship between the sides. Now we go the other way. If the sides of a triangle satisfy that relationship, is there a right angle? We shall see that there is. This gives a test for right angles using only lengths, and it leads to Pythagorean triples and many practical problems with ladders, diagonals and heights.

slides.heading: The converse
slides.body_md: The **converse** of a theorem swaps what is given with what is concluded.

rows: If a triangle has a right angle
If the squares of its sides balance: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$
$\text{then } c^2 = a^2 + b^2 \text{ for the side } c \text{ opposite it}$
then the angle opposite $c$ is a right angle

visual.alt: Table that sets Pythagoras theorem beside its converse. The theorem goes from a right angle to the squares balancing. The converse goes from the squares balancing to a right angle opposite the longest side.

slides.narration: The converse of a theorem swaps what is given with what is concluded. Pythagoras theorem starts with a right angle and concludes that the squares of the sides balance. Its converse starts with the squares balancing, and concludes that there is a right angle, opposite the longest side. A converse is a new statement and needs its own proof, which we give shortly.

slides.heading: Testing a triangle in three steps
slides.body_md: **Converse.** If the square on one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, the angle opposite that side is a **right angle**.

nodes.label: Compare the longest square with the sum of the other two

visual.alt: Flow with three boxes: pick the longest side, square the three sides, compare the longest square with the sum of the other two.
visual.caption: Testing for a right angle

slides.narration: To test a triangle, follow three steps. First, pick out the longest side, because only that side can be the hypotenuse. Second, square all three sides. Third, compare. If the square of the longest side equals the sum of the other two squares, the triangle has a right angle opposite the longest side. If they differ, it has no right angle.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a right-angled triangle
slides.body_md: Is a triangle with sides $28$ cm, $45$ cm and $53$ cm right-angled?
bullets: **Answer —** The squares balance: **right-angled**, the right angle opposite $53$ cm.

visual.alt: A triangle A B C with A B twenty eight, B C forty five and C A fifty three centimetres, with a right angle marked at B.
visual.caption: The test shows a right angle opposite 53 cm.

slides.narration: Test the sides twenty eight, forty five and fifty three. The longest side is fifty three. Twenty eight squared is seven hundred eighty four, and forty five squared is two thousand twenty five. Together they make two thousand eight hundred nine. Fifty three squared is also two thousand eight hundred nine. The squares balance, so the triangle is right angled, with the right angle opposite the side of length fifty three.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: not right-angled
slides.body_md: Is a triangle with sides $14$ cm, $48$ cm and $49$ cm right-angled?

visual.alt: A triangle A B C with A B fourteen, B C forty eight and C A forty nine centimetres. There is no right-angle mark, because the test fails.
visual.caption: Sides 14, 48, 49: no right angle.

slides.narration: Now test fourteen, forty eight and forty nine. The longest side is forty nine. Fourteen squared is one hundred ninety six, and forty eight squared is two thousand three hundred four, and the sum is two thousand five hundred. But forty nine squared is only two thousand four hundred one. The two numbers are different, so this triangle is not right angled. Notice how close the sides are to fourteen, forty eight, fifty, which is right angled.

slides.heading: Quick check: which set works?
slides.body_md: Square, add, compare.
slides.narration: A carpenter has four sets of three battens. Which set can make a right angled frame? For each set, square the two shorter lengths, add them, and compare with the square of the longest.

slides.heading: Why the converse works
slides.body_md: Build a right-angled triangle with the same two shorter sides and compare.

nodes.label: Given: AC squared = AB squared + BC squared
Build triangle PQR: PQ = AB, QR = BC, right angle at Q
PR squared = AB squared + BC squared = AC squared
So PR = AC: the triangles have three equal sides
Congruent, so angle B = angle Q = 90 degrees

visual.alt: Flow with five boxes proving the converse: given the squares balance, build a right-angled triangle P Q R with the same two shorter sides, its hypotenuse equals A C, the triangles are congruent by three equal sides, so angle B is a right angle.
visual.caption: Why the converse works

slides.narration: Why does the converse work? Suppose the squares of the sides of triangle A B C balance. Build a new triangle P Q R with a right angle at Q, and with P Q equal to A B and Q R equal to B C. By Pythagoras theorem, P R squared equals A B squared plus B C squared, which is A C squared. So P R equals A C. The two triangles have three equal sides, so they are congruent, and angle B is a right angle.

slides.heading: Pythagorean triples
slides.body_md: A **Pythagorean triple** is a set of three whole numbers with $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. For $m > n > 0$, the numbers $m^2 - n^2$, $2mn$, $m^2 + n^2$ always form one.

visual.alt: Table of seven Pythagorean triples made from pairs m and n: three four five from two and one, five twelve thirteen from three and two, fifteen eight seventeen, twenty one twenty twenty nine, eleven sixty sixty one, thirty three fifty six sixty five, and ninety one sixty one hundred nine.

slides.narration: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that satisfy the theorem. Take any two whole numbers m and n with m bigger than n. Then m squared minus n squared, two m n, and m squared plus n squared form a triple. The table shows some. With m equal to two and n equal to one we get three, four, five. With m equal to five and n equal to two we get twenty one, twenty, and twenty nine.

slides.heading: Scaling a triple
slides.body_md: **Multiplying** every side by the same number keeps the right angle. **Adding** the same number to every side does not.

visual.alt: Table of four changes to the triple twenty, twenty one, twenty nine: multiplying by two or three or dividing by ten keeps a right angle, but adding five to every side does not.

slides.narration: A triple can be scaled. If every side is multiplied by the same number, the triangle stays right angled, because the squares are all multiplied by the same number. So twenty, twenty one, twenty nine becomes forty, forty two, fifty eight, or sixty, sixty three, eighty seven. Dividing by ten gives two, two point one, two point nine, a right triangle with decimal sides. But adding the same number to every side destroys the balance. Twenty five, twenty six, thirty four is not right angled.

slides.heading: Quick check: make a triple
slides.body_md: Do not forget the two in the middle number.
slides.narration: Use the pattern m squared minus n squared, two m n, m squared plus n squared with m equal to ten and n equal to three. Work out each of the three numbers separately. Take care not to forget the two in the middle number.

slides.heading: The routine for applications
slides.body_md: Real problems hide a right-angled triangle. Find it, then add or subtract squares.

visual.alt: Flow with five boxes: draw a picture, find the right angle, mark the hypotenuse, add or subtract the squares, take the square root and write the unit.
visual.caption: Routine for applications

slides.narration: Every application follows the same routine. Read the problem and draw a picture. Find a right angle, such as a wall meeting the ground, a corner of a rectangle, or the height of an isosceles triangle. Mark the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle. Write the equation, add the squares if you want the hypotenuse, subtract if you want a leg, then solve and write the unit.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a ladder
slides.body_md: A $10.1$ m ladder leans against a vertical wall, with its foot $2$ m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

visual.alt: A ladder leans against a vertical wall. The foot F is 2 metres from the wall base W, the top T is on the wall, and the angle at W is a right angle.
visual.caption: Wall, ground and ladder make a right triangle.

slides.narration: A ladder ten point one metres long leans against a vertical wall with its foot two metres from the wall. How high does it reach? The wall and the ground meet at a right angle, so the ladder is the hypotenuse. Height squared is ten point one squared minus two squared, which is one hundred two point oh one minus four, or ninety eight point oh one. The height is nine point nine metres.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a diagonal of a rectangle
slides.body_md: A rectangular notice board is $9$ cm wide and $40$ cm long. Find the length of its diagonal.

visual.alt: A rectangle A B C D, 9 by 40, with its diagonal A C dashed. Triangle A B C has its right angle at B.
visual.caption: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

slides.narration: A rectangular notice board is nine centimetres wide and forty long. How long is its diagonal? Each corner is a right angle, so the diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs nine and forty. Diagonal squared is eighty one plus one thousand six hundred, which is one thousand six hundred eighty one. The diagonal is forty one centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a diagonal of a square
slides.body_md: A square has side $8$ cm. Find its diagonal.
bullets: **Answer —** $d = 8\sqrt{2} \approx 11.3$ cm. For side $s$ the diagonal is $s\sqrt{2}$.

visual.alt: A rectangle A B C D, 8 by 8, with its diagonal A C dashed. Triangle A B C has its right angle at B.
visual.caption: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

slides.narration: A square has side eight centimetres. Find its diagonal. The diagonal and two sides make a right triangle, so the diagonal squared is eight squared plus eight squared, which is one hundred twenty eight. One hundred twenty eight is sixty four times two, so the diagonal is eight root two centimetres, about eleven point three. For any square of side s, the diagonal is s root two.

slides.heading: Height of an isosceles triangle
slides.body_md: The perpendicular from the apex **bisects the base**. With equal sides $17$ cm and base $30$ cm, each half of the base is $15$ cm.

visual.alt: An isosceles triangle A B C with A B equal to A C. The altitude A M is dashed; it meets B C at right angles at its mid-point M, so B M equals M C.
visual.caption: The altitude of an isosceles triangle bisects the base.

slides.narration: In an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from the apex to the base cuts the base into two equal halves. This gives two right triangles. Here the equal sides are seventeen centimetres and the base is thirty centimetres, so each half base is fifteen. The height squared is seventeen squared minus fifteen squared, which is two hundred eighty nine minus two hundred twenty five, or sixty four. So the height is eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: an equilateral triangle
slides.body_md: Find the height of an equilateral triangle of side $12$ cm.

slides.narration: Now an equilateral triangle of side twelve centimetres. The perpendicular from a vertex cuts the opposite side in two halves of six centimetres. Height squared is twelve squared minus six squared, which is one hundred forty four minus thirty six, or one hundred eight. One hundred eight is thirty six times three, so the height is six root three centimetres. In general the height of an equilateral triangle of side s is s root three over two.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a rhombus
slides.body_md: The diagonals of a rhombus are $32$ cm and $60$ cm. Find its side and perimeter.
bullets: **Step 1 —** The diagonals bisect at right angles: half-diagonals $16$ and $30$.

visual.alt: A rhombus A B C D with its diagonals dashed, meeting at O at right angles. O C is 16 cm and O D is 30 cm. All four sides have one tick mark.
visual.caption: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.

slides.narration: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and bisect each other. Suppose the half diagonals are sixteen and thirty centimetres, so the diagonals are thirty two and sixty. Each side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with those legs. Side squared is two hundred fifty six plus nine hundred, which is one thousand one hundred fifty six. The side is thirty four centimetres, and the perimeter is one hundred thirty six.

slides.heading: Diagonals at right angles
slides.body_md: If the diagonals of $ABCD$ meet at right angles, then $AB^2 + CD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$. Apply the theorem in the four right-angled triangles at $O$. Here $AC = 17$ cm and $BD = 22$ cm.

visual.caption: Diagonals at right angles: four right triangles at O.

slides.narration: Here is a beautiful result. If the diagonals of a quadrilateral cross at right angles, then the squares on one pair of opposite sides add up to the same total as the squares on the other pair. In this quadrilateral the squares of two opposite sides are one hundred thirty and two hundred sixty nine, total three hundred ninety nine. The other pair gives one hundred eighty one and two hundred eighteen, also three hundred ninety nine.

slides.narration: True or false? In a triangle with sides thirty six, one hundred five and one hundred eleven centimetres, the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle. Square the sides, add the two smaller squares, and compare.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a route
slides.body_md: A rescue helicopter flies $33$ km due east and then $56$ km due north. Find its straight-line distance from base, and how much shorter this is than the route flown.
bullets: **Answer —** Route $33 + 56 = 89$ km, so the direct path is $89 - 65 = 24$ km shorter.

sections.heading: 1. The theorem
sections.body_md:
In a right-angled triangle the side **opposite the right angle** is the **hypotenuse**, the longest side; the other two sides are the **legs**.

**Pythagoras theorem.** The square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares on the other two sides: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$.

- It is the **areas of squares** that add: with legs $3$ and $2$ the squares have areas $9$ and $4$, and the square on the hypotenuse has area $13$.
- The lengths do not add: $3 + 2 = 5$, but the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{13} \approx 3.6$.

key_terms.definition_md: The side opposite the right angle in a right-angled triangle; it is the longest side.
The two sides of a right-angled triangle that meet at the right angle.

visual.alt: A right triangle with legs three and two units, with a square drawn outwards on each side. The squares on the legs have areas nine and four; the square on the longest side has area thirteen.
visual.caption: Areas of the three squares: 9 + 4 = 13.

sections.heading: 2. Proof by areas
sections.body_md:
**Construction.** Draw a square of side $a + b$. On each side mark a point so that the pieces are $a$ and $b$ (going round in the same direction) and join the four points. This cuts off four corner triangles with legs $a$ and $b$.

1. The corner triangles are **congruent** (two legs and the right angle between them), so the four slanting sides are all equal to the hypotenuse $c$.
2. In a corner triangle the acute angles $x$ and $y$ satisfy $x + y = 90^\circ$. At each joining point $x$, the angle of the middle shape and $y$ lie on a straight line, so that angle is $180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$. The middle shape is a **square of side $c$**.
3. Count the big square's area two ways: $(a + b)^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2$, that is $a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = 2ab + c^2$, so $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

Check with $a = 20$, $b = 21$: $41^2 = 1681 = 840 + 841$ and $841 = 29^2$.

key_terms.definition_md: Having exactly the same shape and size, so that matching sides and angles are equal.
A helper point or line added to a figure so that a proof can use known results.

visual.alt: The same figure shaded: four right triangles in one shade and the tilted square E F G H in another.
visual.caption: Big square = four triangles + tilted square.

sections.heading: 3. Finding a side
sections.body_md:
- **Hypotenuse (add the squares):** $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$. Legs $2.8$ and $4.5$: $c^2 = 7.84 + 20.25 = 28.09$, so $c = 5.3$.
- **A leg (subtract the squares):** $a = \sqrt{c^2 - b^2}$. Hypotenuse $8.5$, leg $3.6$: $a^2 = 72.25 - 12.96 = 59.29$, so $a = 7.7$.
- **Not a perfect square:** legs $7$ and $9$ give $c^2 = 130$; between $11^2 = 121$ and $12^2 = 144$, so $c = \sqrt{130} \approx 11.40$. Keep the surd for an exact answer and round only at the end.
- **From areas:** squares of areas $289$ (hypotenuse) and $225$ (one leg) give the other leg $\sqrt{289 - 225} = 8$.

key_terms.definition_md: A square root that is not a whole number, such as $\sqrt{130}$, left unsimplified for an exact answer.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle with legs two point eight and four point five centimetres. The hypotenuse is to be found.
visual.caption: Legs 2.8 cm and 4.5 cm.

sections.heading: 4. The converse and the test for a right angle
sections.body_md:
**Converse.** If the square on one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, the angle opposite that side is a **right angle**.

**Proof.** Build $\triangle PQR$ with $PQ = AB$, $QR = BC$ and $\angle Q = 90^\circ$. By the theorem $PR^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$, so $PR = AC$. The triangles have three equal sides, so they are congruent and $\angle B = \angle Q = 90^\circ$.

**Test.** Pick the longest side, square all three sides, and compare the longest square with the sum of the other two.
- $28, 45, 53$: $784 + 2025 = 2809 = 53^2$: **right-angled**.
- $14, 48, 49$: $196 + 2304 = 2500 \neq 2401$: **not right-angled**.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement that swaps what is given and what is concluded in a theorem; it needs its own proof.

visual.alt: A triangle A B C with A B twenty eight, B C forty five and C A fifty three centimetres, with a right angle marked at B.
visual.caption: The test shows a right angle opposite 53 cm.

sections.heading: 5. Pythagorean triples
sections.body_md:
A **Pythagorean triple** is a set of three whole numbers with $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. For $m > n > 0$: $m^2 - n^2$, $2mn$, $m^2 + n^2$ always form one. Examples: $3, 4, 5$; $5, 12, 13$; $20, 21, 29$; $11, 60, 61$; $28, 45, 53$.

- **Multiples** of a triple are triples ($20, 21, 29 \to 40, 42, 58$), and so are decimal versions ($2, 2.1, 2.9$).
- **Adding** the same number to every side destroys the right angle ($25, 26, 34$ is not right-angled).

key_terms.definition_md: Three whole numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ with $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

visual.alt: Table of seven Pythagorean triples made from pairs m and n: three four five from two and one, five twelve thirteen from three and two, fifteen eight seventeen, twenty one twenty twenty nine, eleven sixty sixty one, thirty three fifty six sixty five, and ninety one sixty one hundred nine.

sections.heading: 6. Ladders, routes and diagonals
sections.body_md:
Look for the right angle: a wall meeting the ground, east meeting north, a corner of a rectangle.

- **Ladder** of length $L$ with foot $d$ from the wall: height $= \sqrt{L^2 - d^2}$. A $10.1$ m ladder with its foot $2$ m out reaches $9.9$ m.
- **Route** east $33$ km then north $56$ km: direct distance $\sqrt{33^2 + 56^2} = 65$ km, $24$ km less than the $89$ km flown.
- **Rectangle** $l$ by $b$: diagonal $\sqrt{l^2 + b^2}$ ($9$ by $40$ gives $41$).
- **Square** of side $s$: diagonal $s\sqrt{2}$ ($8$ gives $8\sqrt{2} \approx 11.3$).

key_terms.definition_md: A segment joining two opposite corners of a rectangle or square.

visual.alt: A ladder leans against a vertical wall. The foot F is 2 metres from the wall base W, the top T is on the wall, and the angle at W is a right angle.
visual.caption: Wall, ground and ladder make a right triangle.

sections.heading: 7. Heights, rhombus and perpendicular diagonals
sections.body_md:
- **Isosceles triangle:** the perpendicular from the apex bisects the base. Equal sides $17$ and base $30$: $h^2 = 17^2 - 15^2 = 64$, so $h = 8$.
- **Equilateral triangle** of side $s$: $h^2 = s^2 - \left(\dfrac{s}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$, so $h = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s$. For $s = 12$, $h = 6\sqrt{3}$.
- **Rhombus:** the diagonals bisect at right angles, so $\text{side}^2 = \left(\dfrac{d_1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{d_2}{2}\right)^2$. Diagonals $32$ and $60$ give side $34$.
- **Perpendicular diagonals** of any quadrilateral $ABCD$: $AB^2 + CD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$ (Pythagoras in the four triangles at $O$).

key_terms.definition_md: The perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side.
A quadrilateral with four equal sides; its diagonals bisect each other at right angles.

visual.caption: The altitude of an isosceles triangle bisects the base.

visuals.caption: In an equilateral triangle the altitude also bisects the base.

visuals.caption: Diagonals at right angles: four right triangles at O.

sections.heading: 8. Exam tips and common mistakes
sections.body_md:
**Mark split.** The area proof is marked by step: the figure with side $a + b$ (1), congruent triangles (1), the middle shape is a square with the angle reason (1 or 2), the two area counts (1), the conclusion (1). A converse test: squares (1), comparison and conclusion (1). An application: the right-angled triangle (1), the equation (1), the answer with unit (1).

**Common mistakes**
- Writing $c = a + b$ instead of $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$.
- Adding the squares when a leg is wanted (or subtracting when the hypotenuse is wanted).
- Using a leg as the hypotenuse, or comparing the wrong square in the converse test.
- Adding the same number to every side of a triple and expecting a right angle.
- Not halving the base of an isosceles triangle, or giving $c^2$ as the length.

key_terms.definition_md: The earlier result that justifies a step of a proof.

questions.stem_md: A student writes four statements about $\triangle PQR$, which is right-angled at $Q$. Which one is Pythagoras theorem for this triangle?
questions.solution_md: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, here $PR$. Pythagoras theorem says that the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides: $PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2$. The other statements put the wrong side on the left (for example $PQ$ is a leg), add lengths instead of squares, or subtract.

questions.stem_md: Four identical right-angled triangles with legs $20$ cm and $21$ cm are fitted inside a square of side $41$ cm, one at each corner, so that a tilted square is left in the middle. The area of the tilted square is
questions.solution_md: The big square has area $41^2 = 1681$ and the four triangles have area $4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 21 = 840$, so the tilted square has area $1681 - 840 = 841$ cm$^2$. This is $29^2$, the square on the hypotenuse. The value $840$ is the area of the triangles, $1681$ is the whole square, and $29$ is a length, not an area.

questions.stem_md: A square tile of side $31$ cm has a right-angled triangle cut from each corner, as in the area proof of Pythagoras theorem, leaving a tilted square in the middle. Every cut-off triangle has area $105$ cm$^2$. The area of the tilted square is
questions.solution_md: The tile has area $31^2 = 961$ cm$^2$. The four triangles take $4 \times 105 = 420$ cm$^2$. What is left is $961 - 420 = 541$ cm$^2$. (The legs are $10$ cm and $21$ cm, and $10^2 + 21^2 = 541$.) The value $856$ comes from removing only one triangle, $420$ is the area of all four, and $961$ is the whole tile.

questions.stem_md: In the area proof, four right triangles with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$ sit inside a square of side $a + b$. Which equation comes from counting the area of the big square in two ways?
questions.solution_md: The big square has side $a + b$, so its area is $(a + b)^2$. It is made of four triangles, each of area $\dfrac{1}{2}ab$, and the tilted square of area $c^2$. So $(a + b)^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2$. The other equations mix lengths and areas or leave out the four triangles.

questions.stem_md: In the area proof, a student notices that the four slanting sides of the tilted shape are all equal to the hypotenuse, and says: "That only makes it a rhombus." Which fact shows that the tilted shape is in fact a square?

options.text_md: At each corner the two acute angles of the triangles add up to a right angle, so the angle left on the straight line is a right angle.
All four triangles have the same area, so all four angles of the tilted shape are equal.
The big square has right angles at its corners, so the tilted shape has right angles as well.
Its four sides are equal, and any quadrilateral with four equal sides is a square.

questions.solution_md: Each corner triangle has a right angle and two acute angles $x$ and $y$ with $x + y = 90^\circ$ (angle sum of a triangle). Two of these acute angles and the angle of the tilted shape lie along a straight line, so that angle is $180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$. Equal sides alone give only a rhombus, equal areas say nothing about angles, and the corners of the big square are not corners of the tilted shape.

questions.stem_md: Choose the converse of Pythagoras theorem.

options.text_md: If the angle opposite a side of a triangle is a right angle, the squares on the other two sides are equal.
If the square on one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, the angle opposite that side is a right angle.
If a triangle is right-angled, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.
If the sum of two sides of a triangle equals the third side, the triangle is right-angled.

questions.solution_md: The converse swaps the given fact and the conclusion. The theorem goes from "right-angled" to "$c^2 = a^2 + b^2$", so the converse goes from "$c^2 = a^2 + b^2$" to "the angle opposite $c$ is a right angle". The second option is the theorem itself; the third is false (a triangle cannot have two sides adding up to the third); the fourth is false for most right triangles.

questions.stem_md: A carpenter wants three timber battens to make a right-angled triangular frame. Which set of lengths, in centimetres, should he use?
questions.solution_md: Square the two shorter lengths, add, and compare with the square of the longest. For $48, 55, 73$: $48^2 + 55^2 = 2304 + 3025 = 5329 = 73^2$, so the frame is right-angled. For $48, 55, 75$ the sum is $5329$ but $75^2 = 5625$; for $49, 55, 73$ the sum is $5426$ against $5329$; for $48, 56, 74$ it is $5440$ against $5476$. None of these three balances.

questions.stem_md: A triangular flower bed has sides $3.3$ m, $5.6$ m and $6.5$ m. The angle between the two shorter sides is

options.text_md: impossible to find from the three sides

questions.solution_md: Compare the square of the longest side with the sum of the squares of the other two. In tenths of a metre: $33^2 + 56^2 = 1089 + 3136 = 4225 = 65^2$. The two squares agree, so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle. The angle between the two shorter sides is that angle.

questions.stem_md: The two shorter edges of a right-angled triangular steel plate measure $13$ cm and $84$ cm. The longest edge measures
questions.solution_md: The longest edge is the hypotenuse. $13^2 + 84^2 = 169 + 7056 = 7225$, and $85^2 = 7225$, so it is $85$ cm. The value $97$ comes from adding the lengths, $71$ from subtracting them.

questions.stem_md: A painter leans a $6.1$ m pole against a vertical wall. The foot of the pole is $1.1$ m from the wall on level ground. How high up the wall does the pole reach?
questions.solution_md: The wall, the ground and the pole form a right-angled triangle with the pole as hypotenuse. Height$^2 = 6.1^2 - 1.1^2 = 37.21 - 1.21 = 36$, so the height is $6.0$ m. The value $5.0$ comes from subtracting the lengths, $7.2$ from adding them, and $6.2$ from adding the squares instead of subtracting.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular courtyard is $28$ m long and $45$ m wide. A paved path runs straight from one corner to the opposite corner. The length of the path is
questions.solution_md: The path is the diagonal of the rectangle, the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $28$ m and $45$ m: $28^2 + 45^2 = 784 + 2025 = 2809 = 53^2$. The length is $53$ m. The value $73$ is the sum $28 + 45$ and $17$ is the difference.

questions.stem_md: The diagonal of a square signboard is $14\sqrt{2}$ cm long. The perimeter of the signboard is
questions.solution_md: If the side is $s$, the diagonal squared is $s^2 + s^2 = 2s^2$. Here $2s^2 = (14\sqrt{2})^2 = 392$, so $s^2 = 196$ and $s = 14$ cm. The perimeter is $4 \times 14 = 56$ cm. The value $28$ is only the sum of two sides, $14$ is the side itself, and $56\sqrt{2}$ multiplies the diagonal by four.

questions.stem_md: The two equal sides of an isosceles triangle are $37$ cm each and its base is $24$ cm. The perpendicular from the apex to the base has length
questions.solution_md: The perpendicular from the apex bisects the base, so each half is $12$ cm. In the right-angled triangle formed, $h^2 = 37^2 - 12^2 = 1369 - 144 = 1225$, so $h = 35$ cm. The value $\sqrt{793}$ comes from forgetting to halve the base ($37^2 - 24^2 = 793$), $25$ from subtracting lengths and $49$ from adding them.

questions.stem_md: Every side of an equilateral triangular pennant is $18$ cm. The perpendicular from one vertex to the opposite side is
questions.solution_md: The perpendicular bisects the opposite side, so it splits the triangle into two right-angled triangles with hypotenuse $18$ and a leg $9$. Then $h^2 = 18^2 - 9^2 = 324 - 81 = 243 = 81 \times 3$, so $h = 9\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist rides $0.9$ km due east along a canal and then $4.0$ km due north along a road. How far is she, in a straight line, from her starting point?
questions.solution_md: The two stretches meet at a right angle, so the straight-line distance is the hypotenuse. In tenths of a kilometre: $9^2 + 40^2 = 81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41^2$, so the distance is $4.1$ km. The value $4.9$ comes from adding the stretches and $3.1$ from subtracting them.

questions.stem_md: A rhombus-shaped tile has diagonals of $40$ cm and $42$ cm. Each side of the tile measures
questions.solution_md: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so a side is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $20$ cm and $21$ cm: $20^2 + 21^2 = 400 + 441 = 841$, so the side is $29$ cm. The value $41$ is $20 + 21$, $58$ is twice the side and $82$ is the sum of the diagonals.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of quadrilateral $ABCD$ cross each other at right angles. $AB = 10$ cm, $BC = 17$ cm and $CD = 25$ cm. The length of $AD$ is
questions.solution_md: When the diagonals meet at right angles, $AB^2 + CD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$. So $AD^2 = 10^2 + 25^2 - 17^2 = 100 + 625 - 289 = 436$, and $AD = \sqrt{436} = 2\sqrt{109}$ cm. The value $13\sqrt{6}$ comes from adding all three squares ($1014$) and $\sqrt{814}$ from using $BC^2 + CD^2 - AB^2$.

questions.stem_md: A television mast $118$ m tall and a lighthouse $19$ m tall stand on level ground $20$ m apart. A cable is stretched in a straight line between their tops. The cable is
questions.solution_md: Draw a horizontal line from the top of the lighthouse. It makes a right-angled triangle with legs $20$ m (the distance between the two structures) and $118 - 19 = 99$ m (the difference in heights); the cable is the hypotenuse. $20^2 + 99^2 = 400 + 9801 = 10201 = 101^2$, so the cable is $101$ m. The value $137$ is the sum of the heights and $138$ is $20 + 118$.

questions.stem_md: The hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle is $85$ cm and one of its legs is $36$ cm. The area of the triangle is
questions.solution_md: The other leg is $\sqrt{85^2 - 36^2} = \sqrt{7225 - 1296} = \sqrt{5929} = 77$ cm. The area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 77 = 1386$ cm$^2$. The value $1530$ uses the hypotenuse as a base ($\frac{1}{2} \times 36 \times 85$), $2772$ forgets the half, and $3060$ is $36 \times 85$.

questions.stem_md: A $6.5$ m ladder rests against a vertical wall with its foot $2.5$ m from the wall. The foot is slid outwards until it is $3.9$ m from the wall. By how much does the top of the ladder come down the wall?
questions.solution_md: First position: height $= \sqrt{6.5^2 - 2.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6.0$ m. Second position: height $= \sqrt{6.5^2 - 3.9^2} = \sqrt{27.04} = 5.2$ m. The top comes down $6.0 - 5.2 = 0.8$ m. The value $1.4$ is how far the foot moved, $2.2$ adds the two numbers and $5.2$ is the new height.

questions.stem_md: A triangular metal frame has sides $28$ cm, $45$ cm and $53$ cm. A welder lengthens every side by $3$ cm. The new frame is

options.text_md: right-angled, because every side grew by the same amount
right-angled, because it is still a triangle with its sides in the same order
right-angled, because the longest side is still less than the sum of the other two

questions.solution_md: The old frame is right-angled: $28^2 + 45^2 = 2809 = 53^2$. The new sides are $31$, $48$, $56$, and $31^2 + 48^2 = 961 + 2304 = 3265$ while $56^2 = 3136$. The two squares are different, so by the converse test the new frame has no right angle. Adding the same length to every side does not keep the squares in balance (multiplying every side by the same number would).

questions.stem_md: For $m > n > 0$, the numbers $m^2 - n^2$, $2mn$ and $m^2 + n^2$ always form a Pythagorean triple. Taking $m = 10$ and $n = 3$ gives
questions.solution_md: $m^2 - n^2 = 100 - 9 = 91$, $2mn = 2 \times 10 \times 3 = 60$ and $m^2 + n^2 = 100 + 9 = 109$. Check: $91^2 + 60^2 = 8281 + 3600 = 11881 = 109^2$. Forgetting the factor $2$ gives $91, 30, 109$, which does not balance; $7, 60, 13$ uses $m - n$ and $m + n$; and $100, 9, 109$ uses $m^2$ and $n^2$ as legs.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The square on the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $20$ cm and $21$ cm has area $841$ cm$^2$.

**Reason (R):** In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Assertion: $20^2 + 21^2 = 400 + 441 = 841$, so the square on the hypotenuse has area $841$ cm$^2$ and the assertion is true. Reason: this is Pythagoras theorem, which is true. The reason is exactly why the assertion holds, so the answer is (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A triangle with sides $15$ cm, $36$ cm and $39$ cm is right-angled.

**Reason (R):** A triangle is right-angled whenever the sum of two of its sides equals the third side.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Assertion: $15^2 + 36^2 = 225 + 1296 = 1521 = 39^2$, so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the triangle is right-angled: true. Reason: if two sides added up to the third, there would be no triangle at all (the sides would lie along one line), and the test for a right angle uses squares, not lengths: false. So (A) is true and (R) is false, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A triangle with sides $10$ cm, $24$ cm and $27$ cm is right-angled.

**Reason (R):** If the square on one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, the angle opposite that side is a right angle.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Assertion: $10^2 + 24^2 = 676 = 26^2$, but the longest side is $27$ and $27^2 = 729 \neq 676$, so the triangle is not right-angled: false. Reason: this is the converse of Pythagoras theorem and is true. So (A) is false and (R) is true, option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The diagonal of a square of side $6$ cm is $6\sqrt{2}$ cm.

**Reason (R):** The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Assertion: the diagonal and two sides form a right-angled triangle, so $d^2 = 6^2 + 6^2 = 72$ and $d = 6\sqrt{2}$: true. Reason: true, a standard property of the rhombus. But the assertion follows from Pythagoras theorem on a right angle at a corner of the square, not from the diagonal property of the rhombus, so (R) does not explain (A): option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In an isosceles triangle with equal sides $41$ cm and base $18$ cm, the perpendicular from the apex to the base is $40$ cm long.

**Reason (R):** The perpendicular from the apex of an isosceles triangle to its base bisects the base.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Assertion: the perpendicular splits the triangle into two right-angled triangles with hypotenuse $41$ and base $9$, so its length is $\sqrt{41^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{1600} = 40$ cm: true. Reason: true, and it is the step that gives the base $9$ cm in each right-angled triangle. So (R) explains (A): option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false: in the area proof, the tilted shape left inside the big square is a square whose side is the hypotenuse of each of the four triangles.
questions.solution_md: True. The four triangles are congruent, so the four slanting sides are all equal to the hypotenuse $c$. The acute angles of a triangle add up to $90^\circ$, so each angle of the tilted shape is $180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$. Four equal sides and four right angles make a square of side $c$, and its area is $c^2$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: in a triangle with sides $36$ cm, $105$ cm and $111$ cm, the angle opposite the $111$ cm side is a right angle.
questions.solution_md: True. $36^2 + 105^2 = 1296 + 11025 = 12321$ and $111^2 = 12321$. The squares balance, so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle.

questions.stem_md: True or false: a triangle with sides $14$ cm, $48$ cm and $49$ cm is right-angled.
questions.solution_md: False. $14^2 + 48^2 = 196 + 2304 = 2500 = 50^2$, but the longest side is $49$ cm and $49^2 = 2401$. The squares do not balance, so there is no right angle. (A right-angled triangle with legs $14$ and $48$ would have hypotenuse $50$.)

questions.stem_md: True or false: a rectangular signboard $9$ dm wide and $40$ dm long has a diagonal of $49$ dm.
questions.solution_md: False. The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $9$ dm and $40$ dm, so it is $\sqrt{81 + 1600} = \sqrt{1681} = 41$ dm. The number $49$ is the sum of the sides, and the diagonal is always shorter than the sum of two sides of a triangle.

questions.stem_md: True or false: if every side of a right-angled triangle is multiplied by $3$, the new triangle is also right-angled.
questions.solution_md: True. If $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ then $(3a)^2 + (3b)^2 = 9(a^2 + b^2) = 9c^2 = (3c)^2$, so the new sides satisfy the converse test. For example $20, 21, 29$ becomes $60, 63, 87$ and $60^2 + 63^2 = 3600 + 3969 = 7569 = 87^2$.

questions.stem_md: A right-angled triangle has legs $20$ cm and $99$ cm. Its hypotenuse is ____ cm.
The numbers $12$, $35$ and ____ form a Pythagorean triple (the missing number is the largest).
The longest edge of a right-angled triangular steel plate faces its right angle. Geometers give this edge a special name: the ____.
questions.solution_md: The side opposite the right angle is the longest side of a right-angled triangle; it is called the hypotenuse.

questions.stem_md: A rhombus has diagonals $56$ cm and $90$ cm. Its perimeter is ____ cm.
questions.solution_md: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so a side is the hypotenuse of a triangle with legs $28$ and $45$: $28^2 + 45^2 = 2809 = 53^2$. The perimeter is $4 \times 53 = 212$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Four right-angled triangles with legs $9$ cm and $40$ cm are placed in the corners of a square of side $49$ cm. The tilted square left in the middle has area ____ cm$^2$.
questions.solution_md: The big square has area $49^2 = 2401$ and the four triangles have area $4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 40 = 720$, so the tilted square has area $2401 - 720 = 1681$ cm$^2$ (which is $9^2 + 40^2$).

questions.stem_md: A firefighter rests an $8.9$ m ladder against a vertical wall with its foot $3.9$ m from the wall. How high up the wall does the top of the ladder reach? Answer in metres.

marking_scheme.step: Right-angled triangle with the ladder as hypotenuse: height$^2 = 8.9^2 - 3.9^2$

questions.stem_md: A rectangular lawn is $25$ m long and $18$ m wide. A sprinkler hose is laid along a diagonal. Find the length of the hose, correct to one decimal place, in metres.
questions.solution_md: Diagonal$^2 = 25^2 + 18^2 = 625 + 324 = 949$, so the diagonal is $\sqrt{949} = 30.8$ m (to one decimal place), since $30.8^2 = 948.64$ and $30.9^2 = 954.81$.

questions.stem_md: An equilateral triangular road sign has side $24$ cm. Find its height, correct to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$.) Answer in centimetres.
questions.solution_md: The height splits the base into two halves of $12$ cm. $h^2 = 24^2 - 12^2 = 576 - 144 = 432 = 144 \times 3$, so $h = 12\sqrt{3} = 12 \times 1.732 = 20.784$, which is $20.78$ cm to two decimal places.

questions.stem_md: The sail of a model boat is an isosceles triangle with equal sides $5.3$ cm and base $5.6$ cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
questions.solution_md: The height splits the base into halves of $2.8$ cm: $h^2 = 5.3^2 - 2.8^2 = 28.09 - 7.84 = 20.25$, so $h = 4.5$ cm. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5.6 \times 4.5 = 12.6$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A fishing boat sails $4.8$ km due west and then $5.5$ km due south. How far is it from its starting harbour in a straight line? Answer in kilometres.
questions.solution_md: The two legs of the voyage are at right angles. In tenths of a kilometre $48^2 + 55^2 = 2304 + 3025 = 5329 = 73^2$, so the distance is $\sqrt{53.29} = 7.3$ km.

marking_scheme.step: Right angle between the two legs; $4.8^2 + 5.5^2 = 53.29$

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of quadrilateral $PQRS$ intersect at right angles. $PQ = 15$ cm and $QR = 13$ cm. Find the value of $PS^2 - RS^2$ in square centimetres.
questions.solution_md: With perpendicular diagonals, $PQ^2 + RS^2 = QR^2 + SP^2$. So $PS^2 - RS^2 = PQ^2 - QR^2 = 225 - 169 = 56$. (The two missing sides themselves are not needed.)

questions.stem_md: A rectangular gate frame is $6.5$ ft wide. A diagonal brace across it is $9.7$ ft long. How tall is the frame? Answer in feet.
questions.solution_md: The brace is the hypotenuse, so height$^2 = 9.7^2 - 6.5^2 = 94.09 - 42.25 = 51.84$ and the height is $\sqrt{51.84} = 7.2$ ft (since $72^2 = 5184$).

questions.stem_md: In the square-in-a-square proof, four right-angled triangles with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$ fill the corners of a big square of side $a + b$. Show that counting the area of the big square in two ways gives $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

answer.model_answer_md: The big square has area $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$. It also equals four triangles plus the tilted square: $4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2 = 2ab + c^2$. So $a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = 2ab + c^2$, and cancelling $2ab$ gives $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

questions.solution_md: Area of the big square: $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$. Area as four triangles and the tilted square: $4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2 = 2ab + c^2$. Equate and cancel $2ab$: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

questions.stem_md: Three battens of lengths $24$ cm, $70$ cm and $74$ cm are joined end to end to make a triangle. Is the triangle right-angled? Give a reason, and say which side is opposite the right angle if it is.

answer.model_answer_md: $24^2 + 70^2 = 576 + 4900 = 5476$ and $74^2 = 5476$. The squares balance, so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the triangle is right-angled, with the right angle opposite the longest side, $74$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Square the two shorter sides and add: $24^2 + 70^2 = 576 + 4900 = 5476$. The square of the longest side is $74^2 = 5476$. They are equal, so the triangle is right-angled, and the right angle is opposite the $74$ cm side.

marking_scheme.step: Converse of Pythagoras theorem: right-angled, right angle opposite $74$ cm

questions.stem_md: A signboard is a triangle with sides $8.4$ dm, $11.2$ dm and $14.1$ dm. Is its largest angle a right angle? Show your working.

answer.model_answer_md: $8.4^2 + 11.2^2 = 70.56 + 125.44 = 196$, but $14.1^2 = 198.81$. The two numbers are not equal, so by the converse of Pythagoras theorem the triangle is not right-angled; the largest angle is not a right angle.

questions.solution_md: In tenths of a decimetre: $84^2 + 112^2 = 7056 + 12544 = 19600$ and $141^2 = 19881$. Since $19600 \neq 19881$, the squares do not balance, so the triangle is not right-angled. (The sides $8.4$, $11.2$, $14.0$ would be, but $14.1$ is slightly too long.)

marking_scheme.step: They differ, so the angle is not a right angle

questions.stem_md: A rectangular painting is $12$ in by $19$ in. Find the length of its diagonal, first in exact form and then correct to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $12$ and $19$: $d^2 = 144 + 361 = 505$, so $d = \sqrt{505}$ in. Since $22.4^2 = 501.76$ and $22.5^2 = 506.25$, $d = 22.5$ in to one decimal place.

questions.stem_md: Find the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side $14$ cm, leaving your answer in surd form.

answer.model_answer_md: The altitude bisects the base, so $h^2 = 14^2 - 7^2 = 196 - 49 = 147 = 49 \times 3$, and $h = 7\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The altitude meets the base at its mid-point, $7$ cm from each end, and makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $14$. $h^2 = 14^2 - 7^2 = 147 = 49 \times 3$, so $h = 7\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The diagonal of a square flower bed is $18$ m. Find the side of the bed in surd form.

answer.model_answer_md: Let the side be $s$. Then $s^2 + s^2 = 18^2 = 324$, so $s^2 = 162 = 81 \times 2$ and $s = 9\sqrt{2}$ m.

questions.solution_md: The diagonal and two sides form a right-angled triangle with the diagonal as hypotenuse: $2s^2 = 18^2 = 324$, so $s^2 = 162 = 81 \times 2$ and $s = 9\sqrt{2}$ m.

questions.stem_md: A tent flap is an isosceles triangle with equal sides $20$ dm and base $24$ dm. Find its height from the apex to the base.

answer.model_answer_md: The height bisects the base into two halves of $12$ dm. $h^2 = 20^2 - 12^2 = 400 - 144 = 256$, so $h = 16$ dm.

questions.solution_md: The perpendicular from the apex meets the base at its mid-point, $12$ dm from each end. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $20$: $h^2 = 20^2 - 12^2 = 256$, so $h = 16$ dm.

questions.stem_md: Dev finds the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $24$ cm and $32$ cm and writes: "$24^2 + 32^2 = 576 + 1024 = 1600$, so the hypotenuse is $1600$ cm." Find the mistake and give the correct length.

answer.model_answer_md: Dev found the square of the hypotenuse, $1600$ cm$^2$, but did not take the square root. The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{1600} = 40$ cm.

questions.solution_md: $24^2 + 32^2 = 1600$ is the area of the square on the hypotenuse, not its length. The length is the square root: $\sqrt{1600} = 40$ cm. (Check: $24 : 32 : 40 = 3 : 4 : 5$.)

marking_scheme.step: Mistake: $1600$ is the square of the hypotenuse, no square root taken

questions.stem_md: A support wire $7.3$ m long is fixed to a vertical radio mast at a point $5.5$ m above level ground and pegged to the ground. Find how far the peg is from the foot of the mast, and the perimeter of the triangle formed by the mast (up to the wire), the ground and the wire.

answer.model_answer_md: The mast, ground and wire make a right-angled triangle with the wire as hypotenuse. Distance$^2 = 7.3^2 - 5.5^2 = 53.29 - 30.25 = 23.04$, so the peg is $4.8$ m from the foot. Perimeter $= 5.5 + 4.8 + 7.3 = 17.6$ m.

questions.solution_md: Right angle at the foot of the mast. Peg distance$^2 = 7.3^2 - 5.5^2 = 53.29 - 30.25 = 23.04$, and $4.8^2 = 23.04$, so the distance is $4.8$ m. Perimeter $= 5.5 + 4.8 + 7.3 = 17.6$ m.

questions.stem_md: A rhombus has side $17$ cm and one diagonal $30$ cm. Find the other diagonal and the area of the rhombus.

answer.model_answer_md: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so half of the known diagonal is $15$ cm. Half of the other diagonal $= \sqrt{17^2 - 15^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm, so the other diagonal is $16$ cm. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 16 = 240$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: In the right-angled triangle formed at the centre, the hypotenuse is $17$ and one leg is $15$. The other leg is $\sqrt{289 - 225} = 8$, so the other diagonal is $16$ cm. The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 16 = 240$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio $9 : 40 : 41$ and its perimeter is $270$ cm. Find the sides, show that the triangle is right-angled, and find its area.

answer.model_answer_md: The ratio adds up to $90$ and $270 \div 90 = 3$, so the sides are $27$ cm, $120$ cm and $123$ cm. $27^2 + 120^2 = 729 + 14400 = 15129 = 123^2$, so the triangle is right-angled (converse of Pythagoras theorem). Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 27 \times 120 = 1620$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: $9 + 40 + 41 = 90$, so one part is $270 \div 90 = 3$ cm and the sides are $27$, $120$, $123$ cm. $27^2 + 120^2 = 729 + 14400 = 15129$ and $123^2 = 15129$, so the triangle is right-angled with the right angle between the sides $27$ and $120$. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 27 \times 120 = 1620$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of quadrilateral $ABCD$ intersect at $O$ at right angles. Prove that $AB^2 + CD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$.

answer.model_answer_md: All four angles at $O$ are right angles. Pythagoras theorem in the four right-angled triangles gives $AB^2 = OA^2 + OB^2$, $CD^2 = OC^2 + OD^2$, $AD^2 = OA^2 + OD^2$ and $BC^2 = OB^2 + OC^2$. Adding the first two: $AB^2 + CD^2 = OA^2 + OB^2 + OC^2 + OD^2$. Adding the last two gives the same total, so $AB^2 + CD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$.

questions.solution_md: Since $AC \perp BD$, triangles $AOB$, $BOC$, $COD$, $DOA$ are right-angled at $O$. Then $AB^2 + CD^2 = (OA^2 + OB^2) + (OC^2 + OD^2)$ and $AD^2 + BC^2 = (OA^2 + OD^2) + (OB^2 + OC^2)$. Both equal $OA^2 + OB^2 + OC^2 + OD^2$.

marking_scheme.step: Right angles at $O$; Pythagoras theorem in the four triangles
$AD^2 + BC^2$ equals the same sum, so the two are equal

questions.stem_md: A trail runner jogs $6.0$ km due north from camp, then $9.1$ km due east to a lake. Find the straight-line distance from camp to the lake, and how much shorter this is than the route she ran.

answer.model_answer_md: The north and east legs meet at a right angle. Distance$^2 = 6.0^2 + 9.1^2 = 36 + 82.81 = 118.81$ (in tenths of a kilometre $60^2 + 91^2 = 11881 = 109^2$), so the straight-line distance is $10.9$ km. The route is $6.0 + 9.1 = 15.1$ km, so the straight line is $15.1 - 10.9 = 4.2$ km shorter.

questions.solution_md: Right-angled triangle with legs $6.0$ km and $9.1$ km. Distance$^2 = 6.0^2 + 9.1^2 = 36 + 82.81 = 118.81 = 10.9^2$, so the distance is $10.9$ km. Route $= 15.1$ km, saving $= 15.1 - 10.9 = 4.2$ km.

marking_scheme.step: Right angle between the legs: distance$^2 = 6.0^2 + 9.1^2 = 118.81$

questions.stem_md: The altitude of an equilateral triangular banner is $15\sqrt{3}$ cm. Find the side of the banner and its perimeter.

answer.model_answer_md: Let the side be $s$. The altitude bisects the base, so $h^2 = s^2 - \left(\dfrac{s}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$. Then $(15\sqrt{3})^2 = 675 = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$, so $s^2 = 900$ and $s = 30$ cm. The perimeter is $3 \times 30 = 90$ cm.

questions.solution_md: In the right-angled triangle formed by the altitude, half the base $\dfrac{s}{2}$ and the side $s$: $h^2 = s^2 - \dfrac{s^2}{4} = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$. With $h = 15\sqrt{3}$, $h^2 = 225 \times 3 = 675$, so $s^2 = \dfrac{4 \times 675}{3} = 900$ and $s = 30$ cm. Perimeter $= 90$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
Prove Pythagoras theorem by areas.

(a) Draw a square of side $a + b$ and place four congruent right-angled triangles with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$ in its corners, leaving a tilted shape in the middle. Write the area of each triangle and of the big square. [3]

(b) Prove that the tilted shape is a square of side $c$. [3]

(c) Equate the areas to prove that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, and check the equation for $a = 11$, $b = 60$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) On each side of the big square mark a point that divides it into $a$ and $b$ (going round the square in the same direction), and join the four points. Each corner triangle has legs $a$ and $b$, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{2}ab$. The big square has side $a + b$ and area $(a + b)^2$.

(b) The four triangles are congruent (two legs and the included right angle), so the four slanting sides are all equal to the hypotenuse $c$. In one corner triangle the acute angles $x$ and $y$ satisfy $x + y = 90^\circ$. At each joining point the angles $x$, the tilted shape and $y$ lie along a straight line, so the angle of the tilted shape is $180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$. Four equal sides and four right angles: a square of side $c$ and area $c^2$.

(c) The big square is four triangles plus the tilted square: $(a + b)^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + c^2$, so $a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = 2ab + c^2$ and hence $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. For $a = 11$, $b = 60$: big square $71^2 = 5041$; four triangles $4 \times 330 = 1320$; tilted square $5041 - 1320 = 3721 = 61^2 = 11^2 + 60^2$.

questions.solution_md:
(a) Each triangle has area $\dfrac{1}{2}ab$; the big square has area $(a + b)^2$.

(b) Congruent triangles give four equal sides $c$. The acute angles satisfy $x + y = 90^\circ$ and $x$, the tilted angle and $y$ lie on a straight line, so each angle of the tilted shape is $90^\circ$: it is a square of side $c$.

(c) $(a + b)^2 = 2ab + c^2$ gives $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. For $11$ and $60$: $71^2 = 5041$, $4 \times 330 = 1320$, $5041 - 1320 = 3721 = 61^2$ and $11^2 + 60^2 = 121 + 3600 = 3721$.

questions.stem_md:
Another area proof of Pythagoras theorem uses a big square of side $c$ (the hypotenuse), on whose sides four congruent right-angled triangles with legs $a$ and $b$ ($a < b$) are drawn, with their right angles inside the big square and the hypotenuses along its sides. The four triangles leave a smaller square in the middle.

(a) Show that the side of the smaller square is $b - a$. [3]

(b) Equate areas to prove that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. [3]

(c) Check the result for $a = 28$, $b = 45$, giving the side and the area of the smaller square, the area of one triangle and the value of $c$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At a vertex of the big square the two triangles that meet there have acute angles that add up to $90^\circ$, the angle of the big square. So the long leg $b$ of one triangle and the short leg $a$ of the next lie along one straight line from that vertex. The part of the long leg beyond the short leg has length $b - a$, and this is a side of the middle shape. The four sides of the middle shape are equal to $b - a$, and its angles are right angles because the two legs of each triangle are perpendicular. So it is a square of side $b - a$.

(b) The big square has area $c^2$. It is four triangles plus the middle square: $c^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + (b - a)^2 = 2ab + b^2 - 2ab + a^2 = a^2 + b^2$.

(c) The middle square has side $45 - 28 = 17$ cm and area $17^2 = 289$. One triangle has area $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 28 \times 45 = 630$, and four of them have area $2520$. So $c^2 = 2520 + 289 = 2809$, $c = 53$; and $28^2 + 45^2 = 784 + 2025 = 2809$.

questions.solution_md:
(a) At each vertex of the big square the acute angles of the two meeting triangles add up to $90^\circ$, so the long leg $b$ of one triangle and the short leg $a$ of the next lie on one line. The extra length of the long leg is $b - a$, a side of the middle shape, whose angles are right angles: a square.

(b) $c^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}ab + (b - a)^2 = 2ab + b^2 - 2ab + a^2 = a^2 + b^2$.

(c) Side $17$, area $289$, triangle area $630$, four triangles $2520$, $c^2 = 2809$, $c = 53$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the converse of Pythagoras theorem. [2]

(b) Prove it: in $\triangle ABC$, $AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2$ implies $\angle B = 90^\circ$. [4]

(c) A triangular plot has sides $3.9$ m, $8.0$ m and $8.9$ m. Show that it has a right angle, say between which sides, and find the area of the plot. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) If the square on one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, then the angle opposite the first side is a right angle.

(b) Draw $\triangle PQR$ with $PQ = AB$, $QR = BC$ and $\angle Q = 90^\circ$. By Pythagoras theorem $PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$, so $PR = AC$. Now $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle PQR$ have three equal sides ($AB = PQ$, $BC = QR$, $AC = PR$), so they are congruent (side side side). Hence $\angle B = \angle Q = 90^\circ$.

(c) $3.9^2 + 8.0^2 = 15.21 + 64 = 79.21$ and $8.9^2 = 79.21$, so the squares balance and the angle opposite the $8.9$ m side is a right angle, i.e. between the sides $3.9$ m and $8.0$ m. Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3.9 \times 8.0 = 15.6$ m$^2$.

questions.solution_md:
(a) The converse swaps the given fact and the conclusion of the theorem.

(b) Build a right-angled triangle $PQR$ with legs $AB$ and $BC$. Its hypotenuse is $PR = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2} = AC$, so the two triangles match side side side and $\angle B = 90^\circ$.

(c) $39^2 + 80^2 = 1521 + 6400 = 7921 = 89^2$ (in tenths of a metre), so the right angle is between $3.9$ m and $8.0$ m; area $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 3.9 \times 8.0 = 15.6$ m$^2$.

questions.stem_md:
In quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, $AB = 33$ cm, $BC = 56$ cm, $CD = 60$ cm and $DA = 25$ cm.

(a) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$. [3]

(b) Prove that $\angle ADC = 90^\circ$. [3]

(c) Find the area and the perimeter of $ABCD$. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In right-angled $\triangle ABC$, $AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 = 33^2 + 56^2 = 1089 + 3136 = 4225$, so $AC = 65$ cm.

(b) In $\triangle ADC$, $AD^2 + DC^2 = 25^2 + 60^2 = 625 + 3600 = 4225 = 65^2 = AC^2$. By the converse of Pythagoras theorem $\angle ADC = 90^\circ$.

(c) Area of $\triangle ABC$ $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 33 \times 56 = 924$ cm$^2$; area of $\triangle ADC$ $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 25 \times 60 = 750$ cm$^2$; area of $ABCD = 924 + 750 = 1674$ cm$^2$. Perimeter $= 33 + 56 + 60 + 25 = 174$ cm.

questions.solution_md:
(a) $AC^2 = 33^2 + 56^2 = 4225$, so $AC = 65$ cm.

(b) $25^2 + 60^2 = 4225 = AC^2$, so by the converse $\angle ADC = 90^\circ$.

(c) The diagonal $AC$ splits the quadrilateral into two right-angled triangles: $924 + 750 = 1674$ cm$^2$. Perimeter $= 33 + 56 + 60 + 25 = 174$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
In trapezium $ABCD$, $AB \parallel DC$, $AB = 11$ cm, $DC = 21$ cm and the legs $AD = BC = 13$ cm.

(a) Draw the perpendicular $AM$ from $A$ to $DC$ and find its length. [3]

(b) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$. [3]

(c) Find the area and the perimeter of the trapezium, and state the length of $BD$ with a reason. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) By symmetry $DM = \dfrac{1}{2}(21 - 11) = 5$ cm. In right-angled $\triangle AMD$, $AM^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, so $AM = 12$ cm.

(b) $MC = 21 - 5 = 16$ cm. In right-angled $\triangle AMC$, $AC^2 = 12^2 + 16^2 = 144 + 256 = 400$, so $AC = 20$ cm.

(c) Area $= \dfrac{1}{2}(11 + 21) \times 12 = 192$ cm$^2$. Perimeter $= 11 + 21 + 13 + 13 = 58$ cm. $BD = AC = 20$ cm, because the diagonals of an isosceles trapezium are equal (by the same working with the perpendicular from $B$).

questions.solution_md:
(a) $DM = 5$ cm and $AM = \sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$ cm.

(b) $MC = 16$ cm and $AC = \sqrt{144 + 256} = 20$ cm.

(c) Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 32 \times 12 = 192$ cm$^2$; perimeter $= 58$ cm; $BD = 20$ cm since the perpendicular from $B$ gives the same two legs $12$ and $16$.

questions.stem_md:
$ABC$ is an equilateral triangle of side $16$ cm, and $AM$ is the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$.

(a) Prove that $M$ is the mid-point of $BC$, and find $AM$ in surd form. [3]

(b) Find the area of $\triangle ABC$ in surd form. [3]

(c) Another equilateral triangle has altitude $12$ cm. Find its side and its perimeter in surd form. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In right-angled triangles $AMB$ and $AMC$: $AB = AC$ and $AM$ is common, with right angles at $M$, so the triangles are congruent (right angle, hypotenuse, side) and $BM = MC = 8$ cm. Then $AM^2 = 16^2 - 8^2 = 256 - 64 = 192 = 64 \times 3$, so $AM = 8\sqrt{3}$ cm.

(b) Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 8\sqrt{3} = 64\sqrt{3}$ cm$^2$.

(c) For side $s$ the altitude satisfies $h^2 = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$. With $h = 12$: $144 = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$, so $s^2 = 192 = 64 \times 3$ and $s = 8\sqrt{3}$ cm. The perimeter is $3s = 24\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.solution_md:
(a) Right angle, hypotenuse and a common side make the two right-angled triangles congruent, so $BM = MC = 8$. $AM = \sqrt{256 - 64} = \sqrt{192} = 8\sqrt{3}$ cm.

(b) $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 8\sqrt{3} = 64\sqrt{3}$ cm$^2$.

(c) $144 = \dfrac{3s^2}{4}$ gives $s^2 = 192$ and $s = 8\sqrt{3}$ cm; perimeter $24\sqrt{3}$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ of quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at $O$ at right angles.

(a) Prove that $AB^2 + CD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$. [4]

(b) If $AB = 17$ cm, $CD = 20$ cm and $BC^2 = 208$ cm$^2$, find $AD$ in surd form. [3]

(c) A rhombus $PQRS$ has diagonals $48$ cm and $20$ cm. Find its side and perimeter. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Because $AC \perp BD$, the triangles $AOB$, $BOC$, $COD$ and $DOA$ are right-angled at $O$. By Pythagoras theorem $AB^2 = OA^2 + OB^2$, $CD^2 = OC^2 + OD^2$, $AD^2 = OA^2 + OD^2$ and $BC^2 = OB^2 + OC^2$. So $AB^2 + CD^2 = OA^2 + OB^2 + OC^2 + OD^2 = AD^2 + BC^2$.

(b) $AD^2 = AB^2 + CD^2 - BC^2 = 289 + 400 - 208 = 481$, so $AD = \sqrt{481}$ cm (481 = 13 x 37 has no square factor).

(c) The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so the half-diagonals are $24$ and $10$ and $PQ^2 = 24^2 + 10^2 = 576 + 100 = 676$, so the side is $26$ cm and the perimeter is $104$ cm.

questions.solution_md:
(a) Four right-angled triangles at $O$ and Pythagoras theorem in each, then add in pairs: both sides equal $OA^2 + OB^2 + OC^2 + OD^2$.

(b) $AD^2 = 17^2 + 20^2 - 208 = 481$; $481 = 13 \times 37$, so $AD = \sqrt{481}$ cm.

(c) A rhombus is a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect at right angles: half-diagonals $24$ and $10$, side $\sqrt{676} = 26$ cm, perimeter $104$ cm.
